item.title: US entrepreneurs flocking to Shenzhen does not mean Silicon Valley has 'lost': Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 23:44:00
Skyline of Qianhai area in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province Photo: VCG US entrepreneurs flocking to Shenzhen demonstrates that the natural flow of talent, capital and creative ideas, along with the willingness of the industrial sectors in both China and the US to strengthen cooperation, cannot ultimately be contained, just as the splendor of spring cannot be confined within garden walls. NBC News recently spotlighted an emerging trend in the tech world: a growing number of US tech startups are shifting from Silicon Valley to Shenzhen. According to the report, despite official narratives from Washington deliberately playing up supposed "anxiety" among American companies over China's business environment, US developers, suppliers, and investors are increasingly putting down roots in Shenzhen. There, they are experiencing firsthand the "Shenzhen speed" - where drawings finished at 1 am become physical prototypes by 7 am - alongside a citywide entrepreneurial ethos defined by a readiness to collaborate. Similarly, a Bloomberg video released around the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, which focused on how the city "draws wave of innovators", also drew widespread attention and sparked heated discussion on international social media. The spotlight cast on Shenzhen by international outlets such as NBC and Bloomberg is a microcosm of global media focus on the city around the APEC meeting, and a vivid reflection of how global audiences are seeing and falling in love with Shenzhen through the APEC lens. In truth, these outlets are "late" to the story. They did not "discover" Shenzhen today; rather, Shenzhen has long been shining on the global stage of development and innovation. Where does Shenzhen's magnetic pull come from? By one count, within a two-kilometer radius of Huaqiangbei, known as "China's No. 1 electronics street", there are more than 20 printed circuit board factories, over 10 injection-molding plants, and more than 30 component distributors. With blueprints in hand, a designer can source every necessary component within "a taxi ride's distance" and complete prototyping and testing the very same day. This "Shenzhen cycle" - design in the morning, prototype in the afternoon, mass-produce the next day, and ship globally within a week - never fails to amaze overseas entrepreneurs. A European engineer once completed four iterations of a motor control board prototype in Shenzhen within a single week at a total cost of under $1,000, whereas comparable revisions in Europe would have cost tens of thousands of dollars and taken nearly two months. Locational advantages and industrial clustering dramatically boost R&D efficiency, while supportive policies and a sound business environment provide solid backing. Together, these factors make Shenzhen an ideal habitat for global innovators and entrepreneurs. Shenzhen serves as an important window into China's openness and innovation, and behind Shenzhen stands a dynamic and captivating China. What underpins the "Shenzhen speed" is the seamless flow of production factors across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, supply chain synergy in the Yangtze River Delta, concentrated research resources in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, industrial support from the Chengdu-Chongqing economic zone, and cost-competitive responsiveness from central China. This cross-regional coordination creates a systemic efficiency for "Created in China" that is nearly impossible to replicate. Across its vast expanse, China operates as a massive innovation matrix, with every node brimming with boundless possibilities. For global entrepreneurs, choosing China means choosing an innovation ecosystem where ideas become reality at maximum speed. Here, they enjoy not only the dual advantages of speed and cost, but also the certainty of turning dreams into tangible products. That certainty stems from the strategic depth of China's super-sized market, the resilience and agility of its industrial and supply chains, and a major open economy that keeps its doors wide open to the world. We have also seen a note of self-reflection in US media coverage of Shenzhen, with some reports suggesting that Silicon Valley has invested too heavily in AI and software while losing patience with hardware, leading to an outflow of talent and capital. These are pragmatic observations. However, focusing solely on what Silicon Valley has lost would be somewhat narrow-minded. Shenzhen's appeal lies not in taking something away from others in a zero-sum game, but in opening a window through which innovative ideas from around the world can be translated into reality at lower costs and greater speed before reaching global markets. However, some US politicians and media voices continue to advocate strengthening technological barriers and tightening scrutiny and restrictions on the transfer of technology and products from American companies to China. Such practices create artificial obstacles and erect barriers to their own development. US entrepreneurs flocking to Shenzhen demonstrates that the natural flow of talent, capital and creative ideas, along with the willingness of the industrial sectors in both China and the US to strengthen cooperation, cannot ultimately be contained, just as the splendor of spring cannot be confined within garden walls. Viewed against the broader backdrop of the global economy, Shenzhen's appeal reflects the growing need for innovation resources to flow more freely and be allocated more efficiently worldwide. The International Monetary Fund's latest World Economic Outlook projects that global economic growth will slow to 3.1 percent this year, while global headline inflation will rise to 4.7 percent, with growth forecasts downgraded for nearly half of the world's economies. Sluggish economic growth and mounting business difficulties are increasingly becoming global challenges. At this critical juncture, innovation capacity and industrial momentum are precisely what the world needs most. Behind the sentiment of "I hope my country has its own Shenzhen" lies a desire for more of the spirit of openness and innovation that Shenzhen embodies. China's high-standard opening-up and favorable innovation environment are offering the world precious opportunities and much-needed certainty. Shenzhen's remarkable transformation from a remote fishing village to an international hub of innovation is a vivid microcosm of China's reform and opening-up. Facts have repeatedly demonstrated that decoupling and severing supply chains run counter to popular sentiment and are doomed to fail, while cooperation and development remain the prevailing trends of our times. China will always keep its doors open, offering more opportunities for dreamers around the world to make their dreams come true. Those who choose to embrace this fertile ground for innovation are embracing the future.

item.title: Looking at the China-EU trade deficit from a different perspective
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 23:31:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Chinese goods in the shopping carts of ordinary Europeans represent affordable supplies and reliable choices. Yet in Brussels' trade narrative, they are cast as footnotes of a trade deficit and warning signs of imbalance. Deficits can easily stir up emotions, but do the figures alone equate to real losses? Can a trade balance capture the full truth of China-EU economic and trade relations? Has Europe really gotten the short end of the stick in its trade with China? Moving beyond "deficit anxiety" is key to gaining a fresh understanding of China-EU economic and trade relations. Assessing these ties solely on the basis of the trade deficit overlooks the complexity of bilateral economic links. China-EU economic and trade cooperation has long gone beyond simple buying and selling, forming a community of shared interests in which each side's economy is deeply intertwined with the other's. Beyond trade in goods, alongside China's high-standard opening-up, China-EU trade in services is growing rapidly and becoming an increasingly important component of bilateral cooperation. According to Chinese statistics, China's services trade deficit with the EU reached $48.3 billion in 2025, making the EU China's largest source of services trade deficit, accounting for 41.6 percent of the total. Tens of billions of dollars in intellectual property royalties and other service revenues flow back to Europe each year. These tangible examples of mutually beneficial cooperation have been intentionally or unintentionally obscured by the EU's narrative of a daily 1-billion-euro deficit with China. Looking beyond the figures on the books requires understanding how the benefits are distributed and returning to the essence of trade. Contrary to the picture portrayed by the European side - that China's electric vehicle industry has tucked Europe's traditional auto sector away into a corner - German automaker Volkswagen saw its new energy vehicle deliveries in China rise to 4.5 times their year-earlier level in October, reaching a record 28,000 units. This is a prime example of European automakers actively integrating into Chinese industrial and supply chains and achieving market success. Even as the European Commission continues to push "de-risking" measures targeting China, European companies are voting with their feet. Today, there is widespread worry among European businesses that excessive market intervention by Brussels will drive up operating costs and further weaken Europe's industrial competitiveness. The European side should face up to its own shortcomings rather than blame external factors for its domestic limitations. A growing number of insightful voices in Europe have publicly stated that the "root cause" of Europe's trade imbalance lies within, not beyond its borders, and that blaming China amounts to "treating an internal ailment with external remedies" rather than addressing the problem at its source. Currently, Europe is vigorously advancing its green transition in the hope of boosting its competitiveness, yet at the same time worries about becoming "overly dependent " on Chinese green products - a deeply conflicted mindset. In reality, the China-EU trade gap in the green sector is not the result of unfair competition, but rather a "transition lag" arising from differences in the pace of carbon neutrality efforts and industrial production timelines. The EU's legislative commitment to achieving climate neutrality by 2050 has triggered a sharp short-term surge in demand for green products, while the long construction timelines for capital-intensive production facilities mean that domestic capacity cannot quickly bridge the gap. China's steady supply of cost-effective photovoltaic modules and energy storage equipment has lowered production costs for local European firms, helped stabilize market demand, enabled consumers to save money and strongly supported the EU's energy transition. Blaming others for a temporary supply-demand gap caused by one's own shortcomings not only disregards objective market principles, but also undermines the shared value of China and the EU jointly tackling climate change. Embracing win-win cooperation and working toward a more balanced relationship through dialogue and communication is the way forward. From an economic perspective, a trade deficit does not equate to an economic loss. If one remains fixated on ledger figures, they will fail to properly understand the trade deficit and view it solely as a threat; left unchecked, the deficit narrative risks turning a ledger deficit into a cooperation deficit. Only by looking beyond the deficit and pursuing cooperation can China and the EU achieve greater mutual benefit. The European side should cherish the 16-point consensus outcomes reached at the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism - including those on hybrid vehicle trade - and work with China, in the spirit of mutual respect, equality, and mutual benefit, to take into account each other's core concerns, cultivate new growth drivers for cooperation, and move China-EU economic and trade relations forward toward a more balanced and mutually beneficial relationship. The author is an international affairs observer. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: China's State Council meeting calls for greater role by 'national team' in steadying stock markets
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 23:10:00
stock market Photo:VCG China's key stock indexes surged across the board on Friday, with the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index and the blue-chip CSI300 Index heading for their best session in two years. The surge came after the country convened a State Council executive meeting that urged efforts including giving greater play to "national team" (state-backed) funds in steadying the market. It marks the second time in a month that the State Council executive meeting has issued a dedicated policy direction on the capital market, combined with a series of recent measures to stabilize the stock market, including cutting the minimum stock margin requirement to 80 percent. Chinese experts noted that the measures mentioned at the meeting go beyond a single-dimensional backstop to form a coordinated policy package covering capital supply, trading mechanisms and listed-company quality, which help restore investor confidence, anchor expectations and ultimately serve the market's long-term stability. The meeting also came before the annual Central Economic Work Conference, which, normally held in mid-December, will set out priorities for next year's economic work. Meanwhile, Chinese analysts noted that stabilizing the stock market helps improve market expectations and create a positive cycle of steady investment and consumption, laying the foundation for the country's economy to achieve stable growth. Stabilizing capital market Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Friday chaired a State Council executive meeting. Stressing that the capital market is vital to overall economic development, the meeting called for efforts to strengthen counter-cyclical adjustments and tackle critical reform tasks at the same time, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Efforts should be made to encourage listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share repurchases, give greater play to "national team" (state-backed) funds in steadying the market, and optimize the quasi-"stabilization fund" function of the state-owned Central Huijin Investment Ltd. to provide sufficient liquidity, according to the meeting. "It is worth noting that the timing of the release of the meeting readout differed from the usual after-hours releases, coming just before the A-share afternoon session opened — a move that reflects the policy intent to safeguard market stability and bolster investor confidence," Yang Delong, chief economist at Shenzhen-based First Seafront Fund, told the Global Times on Friday. Against the backdrop of a market that has undergone several months of correction and the growing allocation value of some quality stocks and funds, the meeting's deployment comes as timely relief and is expected to be an important force in driving the market toward stabilization and a rebound, Yang said. During the previous pullback in China's A-share market, the Shanghai Composite Index briefly fell below the 3,500-point psychological threshold, with the pressure stemming partly from the spillover effects of the correction in overseas tech sectors. As of the close on Friday, it reclaimed the 3,600-point mark, closing 3.73 percent higher to end the day at 3,606.49 points, and notching its biggest daily gain since October 2024. The Shenzhen Component Index soared 7.24 percent, the ChiNext Index, tracking China's Nasdaq-style board of growth enterprises, jumped 11.61 percent, while the STAR Composite Index, which reflects the performance of stocks on China's sci-tech innovation board, jumped 14.21 percent. The CSI 300 Index gained 4.17 percent to close at 4,063.06 on Friday, marking its biggest single-day advance since October 2024. Notably, this is the first time the term "national team" has appeared in a readout from a State Council executive meeting, according to an analysis by Xinhua. "It gives the stabilization mechanism a clearer institutional outline, signaling that the market stabilization measures are not temporary but a standing institutional arrangement," Xi Junyang, a professor at the Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, told the Global Times on Friday. According to Xinhua, the meeting also stressed the need to improve market-stabilizing mechanisms, give full play to existing policies, and mull and introduce new measures to promote steady and sound development of the capital market. Over the period, a raft of policies has already been rolled out — optimizing share buybacks and increased holdings, the swap facility, and adjusting the margin requirement ratio. "It now appears that more policy support may be in the pipeline at both the capital market and macroeconomic levels," Xi Junyang said. The meeting also underlined the need to improve policies to support and guide medium- and long-term funds such as insurance funds, enterprise annuities, and social security funds into the market, and strengthen the capacity to guard against and respond to imported risks. "The multiple efforts proposed at the meeting have a positive effect on stabilizing the capital market. Rather than a single-dimensional backstop, these measures form a coordinated policy package spanning capital supply, trading mechanisms, and the quality of listed companies," Xi Junyang said, adding that they point toward enhancing the functions and operational quality of the capital market, helping restore investor confidence, improve market expectations, and deliver an overall benefit for the long-term stability of the capital market. Conducive to stable economic devt Beyond the market itself, the significance of the meeting's deployment extends to the broader macroeconomy, Chinese analysts said. "As the readout made clear from the outset, the capital market is vital to overall economic development — and stabilizing it is not an end in itself, but a means of shoring up expectations, investment and consumption," Tian Yun, a veteran economist based in Beijing, told the Global Times on Friday. According to Tian, the measures are expected to help bolster investor confidence by making clear that while normal corrections are inevitable, the market is on a broadly upward trajectory despite fluctuations. Xi Junyang noted that a healthy capital market can better perform its financing and investment functions and promote the rational allocation of financial resources to more efficient sectors. "This optimization of financial resource allocation, in turn, guides the effective flow of real resources and improves overall operational efficiency, thereby exerting a positive effect on economic growth," he noted. Friday's development also came as official data released on the same day showed that major industrial enterprises recorded an increase of 16 percent year-on-year during the first ten months, with high-tech manufacturing profits surging 50.9 percent. Tian noted that improving corporate earnings provide the fundamental basis for better returns, while a stable capital market helps channel long-term capital into the market to support the development of innovative and tech companies and foster a positive cycle among market stability, corporate development and stable economic growth. Chinese experts also stressed that the strong rebound in China's stock market — particularly the tech-growth segment — coupled with the simultaneous rally in Hong Kong stocks, will help lift risk appetite across Asia-Pacific markets, emerging markets and the broader global market. "As the world's second-largest economy, a recovery in market confidence in China can help reduce part of the global risk premium and may attract some cross-border capital to flow back or reallocate into Chinese assets," Xi Junyang said. Against the backdrop of ongoing volatility in overseas tech markets and shifting global liquidity conditions, as investors worldwide seek a reliable anchor amid uncertainty, China is advancing in a more institutionalized manner to inject a measure of predictable certainty into both its domestic economy and global financial stability, Xi Junyang noted.

item.title: Chinese goods in focus as US Black Friday shoppers seek value amid inflation, tariff pressures
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 22:45:00
People shop at a store during the Black Friday sales event in San Jose, California, the United States, Nov. 28, 2025. (Photo by Ziyu Julian Zhu/Xinhua) As the US Black Friday shopping season gets underway on Friday, persistent inflation is prompting American consumers to seek greater value for money, bringing into focus the competitiveness of Chinese products and the resilience of Chinese cross-border e-commerce businesses amid US tariff pressures. Although US tariffs and the removal of duty-free treatment for low-value imports have increased costs for cross-border e-commerce businesses, interviews with Chinese exporters and industry data point to continued overseas demand as price-sensitive US consumers are still drawn to Chinese goods' affordability and value for money, thanks to China's extensive manufacturing networks, flexible production capabilities and efficient supply chains helping businesses respond to changing consumer preferences and mitigate the impact of trade barriers. Growth under pressure Amid concerns over rising living costs, American consumers have continued to embrace seasonal discounts, with online shopping recording strong growth in the weeks leading up to Black Friday. US consumers spent $82.5 billion online between November 1 and 22, up 9.1 percent year-on-year, the Associated Press (AP) reported on Friday, citing data from Adobe. Online spending on Black Friday alone is projected to reach $12.9 billion, up 9.2 percent year-on-year, according to a forecast released by Adobe Analytics in September, driven in part by having the biggest discounts for categories such as TVs, apparel and appliances. Despite US tariff pressures and high inflation, China's textile and apparel exports to the US rose 20.2 percent year-on-year to $45.49 billion in the first 10 months of this year, accounting for 17.6 percent of China's total textile and apparel exports, according to the latest data provided to the Global Times on Friday by the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Textiles. Major export categories included clothing, home textiles and fabrics, underscoring the continued importance of Chinese products in the American consumer market. Signs of export growth ahead of the Black Friday shopping season were also evident in several home appliance categories. For example, China's air conditioner exports to North America rebounded in October, rising by 6.2 percent, while washing machine exports to the US stabilized after previous declines, edging up 0.5 percent year-on-year. Both improvements were likely driven by inventory stocking ahead of Black Friday, according to data provided to the Global Times on Friday by ChinaIOL, a Chinese industry research and consulting platform. Meanwhile, despite a decline in China's refrigerator exports to the US this year due to tariff barriers, exports recorded a marginal improvement in September, edging up 0.2 percent year-on-year, possibly reflecting advance stocking for the year-end shopping season, according to analysts at ChinaIOL. Tao Yang, a businessperson from Yiwu, the "world's supermarket" in East China's Zhejiang Province, echoed the positive trend. "Our orders from the US market this year have increased by an estimated 50 percent compared with last year, partly because our products cater to emerging consumer trends on social media," Tao, CEO of Yiwu KiviBear Household Products Co Ltd, told the Global Times on Friday. The Yiwu-based businessperson said that her company's main products for this year's Black Friday shopping season are decorative accessories for drinking cups, which allow consumers to personalize everyday items. Tao said that when household budgets are under pressure, consumers tend to favor affordable products over big-ticket purchases, a phenomenon known as the "lipstick effect." Such a shift in spending habits is particularly relevant in the US, where persistent inflation continues to weigh on consumer purchasing power. According to a Reuters report on Friday, US holiday spending is expected to rise by 4 to 6 percent from last year, with rising prices accounting for much of the expected growth. US inflation currently stands at 3.8 percent. A November survey by the US National Retail Federation found that 82 percent of US consumers are taking steps to manage holiday shopping costs, according to Reuters. The potential for Chinese suppliers to tap into holiday demand is reinforced by the substantial consumer base that Chinese cross-border e-commerce platforms have established in the US. A survey released in March by e-commerce marketing company Omnisend found that 71 percent of US respondents had made purchases on one or more Chinese online marketplaces, including Temu, SHEIN, AliExpress and TikTok Shop, during the previous year. As American consumers become more price-conscious, Chinese products that offer good value for money could gain a competitive edge in the US market, He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, told the Global Times on Friday. Moreover, the competitiveness of Chinese goods extends beyond price advantages. China's extensive manufacturing networks, economies of scale and efficient supply chains enable businesses to offer a wide range of affordable, high-quality products while responding rapidly to evolving consumer preferences, He said. Adapting to changes US tariffs and the removal of duty-free treatment for low-value imports last year have posed challenges to Chinese cross-border e-commerce businesses, prompting them to adapt their business models to a changing trade environment. "These policy changes have increased import costs and disrupted established cross-border retail models, prompting businesses to adjust their operations, expand local fulfillment capabilities and improve supply chain efficiency," said He. Despite these challenges, Chinese cross-border e-commerce platforms continue to attract American consumers. Temu, for example, attracted 108.2 million unique visitors in the US in June 2026, up 79 percent year-on-year, according to a September report by market research firm EMARKETER, citing data from Comscore. Beyond adjustments in logistics and business models, China's flexible manufacturing capabilities and efficient supply chains have enabled Chinese suppliers to better respond to changing consumer demand, providing another source of resilience amid trade uncertainties, industry analysts said. Tao said American customers are increasingly seeking distinctive products and placing small initial orders to test market demand before scaling up purchases, sometimes even opting for air freight to expedite delivery. Thanks to its well-integrated supply chain, Tao's company can accommodate small customized orders and arrange rapid deliveries. Over the past two weeks, the company has been rushing to fulfill orders, with some customers requesting delivery as early as the day after placing their orders. While Chinese businesses continue to demonstrate resilience and adaptability in the face of trade barriers, Washington's renewed tariff push has drawn fresh concerns from the Chinese business community over its potential impact on businesses and consumers on both sides. On Friday, the Chinese business community urged the US to withdraw its proposed Section 301 tariff hikes and resolve outstanding issues through consultations. A spokesperson for the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) warned that sweeping tariff increases would raise costs for downstream US businesses, place additional financial pressure on consumers and disrupt global industrial and supply chains. The continued demand for affordable Chinese products during the Black Friday shopping season underscores the strong economic rationale for China-US trade cooperation. The competitiveness of Chinese products stems not just from their prices, but also from the efficiency of an extensive industrial ecosystem built up over decades, Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Friday. For many American households already struggling with rising living costs, additional tariffs risk putting affordable goods further out of reach, Hu said. He noted that stable China-US trade relations, rather than higher trade barriers, would better serve the interests of American consumers and businesses on both sides.

item.title: Hong Kong completes adaptation of pre-1997 laws, marking milestone in 'one country, two systems': expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 22:14:00
Members of the Hong Kong Police guards of honor raise the Chinese national flag and HKSAR flag during a ceremony at the Golden Bauhinia Square in Hong Kong, China, on July 1, 2026, marking the 29th anniversary of Hong Kong's return to the motherland. Photo: VCG The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) on Friday completed the adaptation of more than 1,800 laws that were in force before Hong Kong's return to the motherland, marking a major milestone in the practice of "one country, two systems" and resolving the longstanding issue of decolonization in its pre-1997 laws, according to a commentary published by the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office of the State Council on Friday. According to an official release from the HKSAR government on Friday, the completion of the exercise came as the Statute Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance 2026 and the subsidiary legislation that amends the rules of court, namely the Rules of the High Court (Amendment) (No. 3) Rules 2026, the High Court Fees (Amendment) Rules 2026 and the Rules of the District Court (Amendment) (No. 3) Rules 2026, were published in the Gazette on Friday. The government said that the gazetting of the ordinance and subsidiary legislation marked the formal completion of the historic mission of the adaptation exercise, seven months ahead of the original deadline at the end of current government's term. A spokesperson for the Liaison Office of the Central People's Government in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) said in a statement on Friday that HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee and the local government had taken proactive steps and accelerated the adaptation of Hong Kong's previously existing laws. The spokesperson said the ahead-of-schedule completion fully demonstrated the considerable advantages of Hong Kong's executive-led system following the implementation of the principle of "patriots administering Hong Kong" under the safeguards of the Basic Law and the National Security Law for Hong Kong. The commentary noted that adapting Hong Kong's previously existing laws is an inevitable requirement arising from China's resumption of the exercise of sovereignty over Hong Kong and a constitutional duty that the HKSAR must fulfill. The exercise has eliminated colonial-era expressions and vestiges of colonial privileges from these laws, further consolidating the legal foundations of "one country, two systems." The completion of the adaptation exercise means Hong Kong's laws now directly reflect the HKSAR's constitutional status without relying on substitution rules, marking a historic transition from colonial governance to the HKSAR's constitutional order. It further strengthens the common law system within the national constitutional framework and marks a milestone in the practice of "one country, two systems," Willy Fu, a law professor who is also a director of the Chinese Association of Hong Kong & Macao Studies, told the Global Times on Friday. The HKSAR government began adapting the laws following Hong Kong's return to the motherland, completing more than 90 percent of the amendments by 2012. However, the subsequent progress was slowed by anti-China, destabilizing forces in Hong Kong that used the Legislative Council to obstruct the government's efforts, the commentary said. The completion of the adaptation of laws has also strengthened the advantages of Hong Kong's common law system by eliminating ambiguities and disputes over the application of laws arising from previous reliance on statutory substitution rules, according to the commentary. The adaptation removes colonial-era references from legal texts, not the common law itself. By directly reflecting the HKSAR's constitutional status, the amended laws enhance judicial efficiency and legal certainty, allowing Hong Kong's common law system to better leverage its strengths in the international legal arena, Fu said. The exercise has also aligned certain industry standards in Hong Kong's commercial and maritime sectors with national standards and internationally accepted rules, which will help strengthen Hong Kong's position as an international legal hub and boost international investors' confidence in its rule of law and business environment, the commentary said. Clearer legal texts help reduce legal interpretation costs in areas like due diligence and contract drafting. The systematic completion of the adaptation exercise also signals to international markets that Hong Kong's legal system can evolve in an orderly manner, reducing legal uncertainty for long-term investment and improving international investors' assessment of Hong Kong's risk profile as a legal hub, Fu said. As Hong Kong approaches the 30th anniversary of its return to the motherland, the completion of the adaptation of its previously existing laws is of profound significance for the full and accurate implementation of the "one country, two systems" policy and the Basic Law, the commentary noted.

item.title: Foreign carmakers tap Chinese tech in global market push
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 21:52:00
Visitors tour the 24th Guangzhou International Automobile Exhibition at the China Import and Export Fair Complex in Guangzhou, South China's Guangdong Province, on November 27, 2026. The show, themed "New Tech, New Life," covers 220,000 square meters and features 1,106 vehicles, including 115 making their debut and 707 new-energy vehicles. Photo: VCG From Dongfeng Nissan exporting its China-developed N7 electric sedan to Southeast Asia to Volkswagen showcasing cars built on an electronic architecture co-developed with Chinese partners, the 24th Guangzhou International Automobile Exhibition, known as the Guangzhou Auto Show, which opened Friday, highlighted how Chinese buyers' preferences are shaping foreign carmakers' global offerings. Analysts said China's engineering and supply chains help foreign brands respond more quickly to local demand and compete abroad. Dongfeng Nissan's NX7, a plug-in hybrid SUV launched at the show for younger buyers, comes with a battery supplied by Chinese firm CATL, as well as intelligent driver assistance and a digital cockpit. An earlier model in the same series has already made the trip overseas. The all-electric N7, developed and built in China, debuted at the Guangzhou show in 2024 and went on sale in China the following year. The first batch bound for Southeast Asia was shipped in September, according to Nissan. The company also plans to launch the N7 in Latin America. At Volkswagen's stand, FAW-Volkswagen delivered its 20,000th ID. AURA T6 model, according a statement sent to the Global Times from the joint venture. The electric SUV and the ID. AURA L5 sedan on display both use the CEA (China Electronic Architecture), which coordinates the vehicles' electronic systems and supports over-the-air software updates. Volkswagen's China technology and software teams developed the architecture with Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker XPENG. The companies have extended their collaboration to Volkswagen's plug-in hybrid and combustion-engine platforms in China, according to XPENG. "In the past, they traded technology for market access," Zhang Xiang, a visiting professor in the engineering department of Zhengzhou-based Huanghe Science and Technology University, told the Global Times on Friday. Now, foreign automakers are paying for technology or using equity partnerships to gain access to Chinese expertise, he said. Developing batteries, digital cockpits and driver-assistance systems independently takes time and several rounds of testing. "Working with Chinese suppliers can help foreign brands bring those technologies to their cars faster," he said. The technology is also being adopted in vehicles with different powertrains. Mercedes-Benz launched a 48-volt hybrid CLA model equipped with the same driver-assistance system as its all-electric counterpart, jointly developed with China's Momenta, according to a statement from the company. Its electric VLE MPV also made its China debut with a rear entertainment system developed under the leadership of Mercedes-Benz's China R&D team. Hybrids allow established carmakers to continue using their existing engine technology while improving fuel economy, Zhang said. He added that stricter fuel-consumption and emissions requirements are another reason foreign brands are continuing to introduce hybrid models alongside all-electric models. BMW launched its long-wheelbase Neue Klasse i3 in Guangzhou, a battery-electric sedan developed specifically for the Chinese market and priced from 249,900 yuan ($37,497). China also supplies vehicles for BMW's global lineup. According to a statement from BMW, Spotlight Automotive, its joint venture with Great Wall Motor, produces electric MINI Cooper and MINI Aceman models for global markets at its plant in Zhangjiagang, East China's Jiangsu Province. Volkswagen's October deliveries offer an early indication of how its locally developed models are faring in China. The Volkswagen brand delivered more than 28,000 new-energy vehicles in China in October, up 346.9 percent year-on-year and a monthly record, according to figures the company released on November 11. The ID. AURA T6 accounted for more than 12,000 deliveries, while the ID. ERA 5S plug-in hybrid sedan contributed another 7,100. Wu Shuocheng, an auto industry expert, told the Global Times on Friday that adopting Chinese EV technology was an important factor behind the increase in sales. Volkswagen's early ID. models had lagged behind Chinese rivals in software responsiveness and the breadth of cockpit features, he said. As Volkswagen has shifted more software development to China, it has been "gradually finding its rhythm." Wu said foreign brands retain strengths in mechanical engineering and established brand equity. Keeping pace with Chinese consumer preferences also requires giving local teams greater room to make product decisions, he said. The shift was visible in Hefei, East China's Anhui Province, on October 27, the first day of German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's state visit to China . Steinmeier toured Volkswagen Group's largest research and development center outside Germany and tried out driver-assistance and automated parking features on locally developed vehicles, according to China Central Television. He later said he was pleased to see German and Chinese engineers developing automotive software together and called for closer cooperation between companies from both countries, according to a report by Xinhua News Agency. A Reuters' report said in October that Volkswagen has announced plans to ship more China-built Volkswagen and Jetta cars to South America and Africa in the coming years. Other auto giants including General Motors, Hyundai and Renault are increasingly adopting similar strategies to globalize their China-developed technologies as they vie with Chinese competitors in international markets, Reuters said. Wu said the experience foreign automakers gain in China can help them compete overseas as other markets move toward electrification. "If a carmaker can't gain a foothold in China's EV market, it will also find it difficult to carve out a place for itself in the global shift to electric vehicles," he said.

item.title: Japan pushes for substantial increase in defense spending; expert warns of shift toward offensive military capability
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 20:15:00
Protesters hold up signs as they listen to speakers during a rally against the current government across the street from the National Diet in Tokyo on August 19, 2026. Photo: VCG Japan is considering allocating 56.3 trillion yen ($353.4 billion) for defense spending over the next five years, a substantial increase from its current five-year plan, as Tokyo pushes ahead with a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities. The move, alongside a series of recent military pushes, reflects Japan's accelerating shift away from its long-held "exclusively defense-oriented policy" toward developing both offensive and defensive military capabilities, a Chinese military expert said, warning that the buildup could heighten security risks. The Japanese government is considering the 56.3 trillion yen figure for the five years starting in fiscal 2027, up from the 43 trillion yen allocated under the current five-year framework, the Asahi Shimbun reported on Friday, citing government sources. The spending amount is expected to be reflected in early revisions to the country's three security documents, which are scheduled to be completed by the end of this year, according to the report. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had expressed her intention to revise the documents a year earlier than scheduled to significantly bolster Japan's defense capabilities amid an increasingly severe international security environment, per Asahi Shimbun. Specifically, the plan could feature large purchases of drones, missile procurement and improvements in Japan's ability to sustain military operations, Jiji News reported. Zhang Junshe, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Friday that the planned spending and the weapons procurement it would support reflect a shift in Japan's military strategy from its long-held "exclusively defense-oriented policy" toward a combination of defensive and offensive capabilities. Zhang said these priorities point to a broader change in the nature of Japan's military buildup. Rather than focusing solely on equipment upgrades or responding to immediate security contingencies, Tokyo is developing capabilities intended to support longer-term military operations, including logistics, supply and infrastructure resilience. This, he said, reflects a shift toward more comprehensive war preparations. Beyond the expansion of military capabilities outlined in the spending plan, Japan has also been pursuing policy changes that could provide broader support for its military buildup. Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) recently claimed that the possibility of acquiring nuclear-powered submarines has not been ruled out from the outset as Japan prepares to revise its three security documents by the end of this year, the Asahi Shimbun reported on November 23. Japan is also considering measures to strengthen its domestic defense industry and promote arms exports. The Japanese government is considering establishing a government-backed entity to purchase defense equipment from domestic manufacturers and sell it to overseas customers, the Yomiuri Shimbun reported on November 17. Zhang said that, taken together, Japan's moves suggest that its military buildup is becoming increasingly systematic. He also warned that such developments could increase military pressure on neighboring countries and fuel a regional arms race, raising the risks of miscalculation and confrontation. Japan's rapid push to revise the three security documents, boost military expenditure and develop offensive capabilities says a lot about its agenda to speed up remilitarization, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on November 5, in response to a question about the Japanese government's approval to update its three security documents in December. Guo said that historically, Japanese militarists committed horrendous crimes and inflicted immense suffering on people in the Asia Pacific and beyond. The lessons are still fresh and must not be forgotten. Japan's reckless remilitarization and repeated breach of its "exclusively defense-oriented" policy seriously threaten regional peace and stability, and challenge the postwar international order. The international community must stay on high alert and jointly push back against this dangerous tendency, he added. Zhang Ruiqi contributed to the story

item.title: ITU adopts first-ever resolution on spectrum use for lunar exploration; move to ease spectrum conflicts, boost intl co-op: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 19:51:00
A full moon is pictured in Harbin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, Dec. 4, 2025. This year's second-largest full moon to the eyes of lunar observers will appear on Friday morning, but the best viewing time falls on Thursday evening. (Xinhua/Zhang Tao) A new resolution on lunar exploration, jointly submitted by China, Russia and Brazil, was formally adopted at the 2026 Plenipotentiary Conference of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the global body responsible for managing radio-frequency spectrum and satellite orbits, on Thursday. Analysts believe it will not only boost cross-border scientific collaboration on lunar exploration, but also mark a major breakthrough for China's efforts to play a deeper role in formulating international rules governing radiocommunication in Earth‑Moon space. Calling for innovative radiocommunication solutions to support lunar missions, the resolution is the first of its kind dedicated to lunar exploration adopted by ITU's highest decision-making body. ITU's official release described it as a "landmark" document. According to the ITU, potential areas for innovation include technical and regulatory frameworks to enable communications between systems operating on the lunar surface and in lunar orbit. The resolution also promotes efficient spectrum utilization, compatibility with existing radiocommunication services, and protection against harmful interference. Mario Maniewicz, Director of the ITU Radiocommunication Bureau, said the resolution highlights the essential role of radio services for nearly all activities carried out by humans or robots on and around the Moon. It calls for further technical studies on communications between surface and orbital systems, including sophisticated spectrum-sharing arrangements for different radio services. Radio frequencies are essential to lunar missions, supporting applications such as communications, navigation and remote sensing. ITU governs radiocommunication activities for lunar exploration under the Radio Regulations, the international treaty governing the global use of radio-frequency spectrum and associated satellite orbits. To date, 10 countries have submitted radio frequency filings for projects on or around the Moon, according to the ITU. Chinese aerospace expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times on Friday that radio spectrum is a scarce strategic electromagnetic resource with limited capacity across specific time, space and frequency bands. Adjacent frequency bands used simultaneously in the same location are highly susceptible to electromagnetic interference. Moreover, the great distance between Earth and the Moon requires dedicated deep-space frequency bands to be reserved and protected from interference originating from Earth and other signal sources. "This necessitates unified planning and allocation by the ITU," Song added. The expert noted the resolution will lower the risk of mutual interference among lunar exploration missions of different countries and reduce spectrum conflicts. "It will also boost cross-border scientific collaboration on lunar exploration, enabling joint observation and data sharing among lunar payloads and relay satellites from various nations," Song said. "It will promote interoperability among deep-space communication standards and protocols, paving the way for future initiatives including the joint construction of lunar research stations and multinational crewed lunar landing missions." The resolution also represents a major breakthrough in China's active participation in formulating international rules governing radiocommunication in the Earth-Moon space, analysts said. Radio-frequency spectrum resources are shared deep-space resources belonging to all humankind and should be equally accessible for all nations, said Song, noting that unilateral appropriation and exclusion should be opposed and that rules governing their use should be jointly formulated by all countries.

item.title: Pakistani minister praises Chinese public's warm send-off for Shenzhou-24 crew, China's willingness to share its success
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 23:21:00
Pakistani minister praises Chinese public's warm send-off for Shenzhou-24 crew, China's willingness to share its success By Dong Feng and Li Yu Published: Nov 26, 2026 11:21 PM Updated: Nov 26, 2026 11:33 PM Professor Ahsan Iqbal (left), Pakistan's Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives, speaks at a media talk in the Pakistan Embassy in Beijing, on November 26, 2026. Photo: Dong Feng / Global Times Following China's successful launch of the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft on Wednesday, sending three astronauts, including a Pakistani astronaut, into the orbiting Tiangong space station, Pakistan's Federal Minister for Planning, Development & Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal spoke at a media event on Thursday where he highlighted the warm farewell for the departing astronauts, and the enthusiastic cheers from the Chinese people for the Pakistani astronaut at the send-off ceremony, and a distinctive feature of China's development policy: its willingness to share its success with other countries. Iqbal said the scientific experiments to be conducted by Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali aboard China's Tiangong space station could help Pakistan address food security challenges. The research would provide Pakistani scientists with insights into developing smart agriculture and weather-resistant seed varieties, while materials science experiments could also help strengthen the country's industrial capabilities. He said collaboration with China and future satellite launches could also strengthen Pakistan's satellite navigation capabilities, with applications in water management, agriculture, urban planning, logistics and connectivity. More than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests are planned for the Shenzhou-24 mission, covering space life sciences, space material science, microgravity fluid physics and combustion science, fundamental physics, space medicine and new space technologies, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). Four China-Pakistan cooperative projects in the fields of biotechnology and materials will be conducted during the Shenzhou-24 mission, and the Pakistani payload specialist Ali will conduct an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria, which was proposed by the Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), the Xinhua News Agency reported. Iqbal said space technology had become an integral part of national development planning, warning that countries that failed to acquire emerging technologies would struggle to compete in the future. He described cooperation with China as timely, saying it would provide Pakistan with critical knowledge and capabilities to harness new technologies for the benefit of its people. Iqbal described the mission as another flagship project of Pakistan-China cooperation, extending a partnership built through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) on the ground into space. China-Pakistan space cooperation spans more than three decades. In 1990, Pakistan's first experimental satellite, Badr-1, was launched aboard a Chinese rocket from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center. More recently, China launched Pakistan's cube satellite aboard the Chang'e-6 probe in 2024 and placed a Pakistani remote-sensing satellite in orbit via a Long March-6 rocket in April 2026, according to Xinhua. Looking beyond space cooperation, Iqbal said Pakistan and China were discussing the need for a knowledge corridor to prepare Pakistan's younger generation for emerging technologies. He said the government's Uraan Pakistan agenda placed a high priority on equipping young people with the skills and knowledge needed for Industrial Revolutions 4.0 and 5.0. Pakistan's National Economic Transformation Plan 2024-29, known as Uraan Pakistan, focuses on exports, equity and empowerment, environment, food and water security, energy and infrastructure, while the country's government will focus on growing industry, commerce and information technology, according to Xinhua. Pakistan hopes to have at least 10,000 PhD students receive training at top Chinese universities over the next 10 years in fields including artificial intelligence, space sciences, materials science, biotechnology, big data, automation and robotics, Iqbal said. The initiative aims to prepare a new generation of researchers, scientists and leaders who can drive Pakistan's future development. Answering a question from the Global Times about the alignment between China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) and Pakistan's development agenda, Iqbal said the two were well aligned. Under the second phase of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, known as CPEC 2.0, Pakistan had identified five cooperation corridors: growth, livelihoods, innovation, green economy and openness to broader regional cooperation. Iqbal also cited space exploration as an example of advanced-science cooperation, noting that an agreement signed in February 2025 had been put into practice through the participation of a Pakistani astronaut in the Shenzhou-24 mission in November 2026. He said Pakistan hoped to further cooperate with China in space exploration, including drawing on China's planned crewed lunar landing before 2030 as Pakistan works toward its own lunar landing goal by 2035. "I think that is the uniqueness of China's policy of development, that it is willing to share its successes with other countries," Iqbal said, recalling his experience at the send-off ceremony, the warmth and the affection that Chinese people expressed when saying goodbye to the departing astronauts. Iqbal said what really impressed him was that thousands of Chinese people had gathered to farewell to the astronauts. "So that really reflected the special bond between China and Pakistan, not just at the government level, but also at the people-to-people level... Every media channel has covered it [the Shenzhou-24 mission] from East to West, and everyone is talking about it and appreciating China's commitment toward sharing its successes with the developing countries and Global South, and particularly with Pakistan. And this opens a new avenue of collaboration between Global South and China in many fields," Iqbal said.

item.title: GT Voice: India's construction equipment localization drive should not be trapped in an anti-China narrative
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 22:28:00
China-India industrial cooperation potential Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT India's Union Cabinet has approved an eight-year industrial support program with a total outlay of 110 billion rupees ($1.19 billion). The initiative aims to improve the country's manufacturing of construction and infrastructure equipment (CIE) and its components, as well as establish a dedicated CIE testing facility, thereby enhancing self-reliance and positioning India as a key player in the global CIE market. However, some Indian media outlets have linked this industrial support policy to claimed concerns over the supply of Chinese equipment. The Economic Times said that the move comes amid "China's restrictions on exports of certain heavy equipment, including tunnel boring machines." India's business news channel CNBC TV18 interpreted the plan as "part of the government's broader push to build domestic manufacturing capacity and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers." It added that India largely depends on China for these machines, which are used in infrastructure projects in hilly, high-altitude and border areas. India's development of its construction equipment industry has its own economic logic, and there is no need to link a normal process of industrialization to a "de-China" or an "anti-China" narrative. According to some media reports, approval of the plan followed nearly two years of discussions between the construction equipment industry and the government on financial incentives to boost domestic manufacturing. This shows that the industry's underlying economic rationale long predates recent supply concerns. As a developing economy undergoing rapid industrialization and urbanization, India's desire to build a domestic construction equipment industry is not hard to understand. As construction of roads, railways, ports and other infrastructure continues, demand for construction equipment in India keeps growing. India is the world's third-largest market for CIE, after China and the US. Indian government figures put the market at about 975 billion rupees ($11 billion) in fiscal year 2024-25. Fueled by rapid growth in infrastructure and housing, it is projected to more than double to roughly 2.28 trillion rupees by fiscal 2029-30. This vast market demand provides a practical foundation for nurturing indigenous manufacturing capacity. China has no reason to see India's industrial progress as a threat. What truly warrants caution is that some Indian manufacturers are trying to secure more market space for local production by imposing tariffs and tightening local sourcing requirements. High-end construction equipment is technology-, capital- and supply-chain-intensive. Its production involves precision machinery, hydraulic systems, core components, industrial controls and many other components. Erecting trade barriers while India's supporting industrial base is still immature may drive up equipment procurement and production costs, potentially slowing the country's ambitious infrastructure build-out. The concerns expressed by multinational manufacturers operating in India deserve to be taken seriously. How to turn vast domestic market demand into a competitive edge for local manufacturing is a challenge shared by many developing countries still undergoing industrialization. China's CIE also went through a stage when its technological foundations were weak and it relied heavily on imported core components. The path it took to upgrade could offer useful lessons for India. Looking back at the development of China's CIE, opening-up and cooperation, on the one hand, and independent innovation, on the other, have always been two mutually reinforcing main threads. In the 1980s, Chinese construction equipment companies introduced advanced foreign technologies on a large scale. Take Chinese leading construction equipment maker company LiuGong as an example. The company introduced technology from US-based Caterpillar in 1987 and formed a joint venture with Germany's ZF Friedrichshafen AG in 1995. It then steadily strengthened its research and development (R&D) efforts and gradually built an industrial system covering complete machines, core components and services. In recent years, Chinese construction equipment companies have made breakthroughs in electrification, intelligent technologies and other fields. This development path shows that international cooperation does not necessarily lead to technological dependence, and that opening markets does not mean giving up independent innovation. The key lies in whether international technologies and industrial resources can be effectively combined with a country's own R&D capabilities, market demand and engineering practice, so that external resources become endogenous drivers of development. As the global construction equipment industry accelerates its shift toward intelligent and green technologies, China and India still have broad room for cooperation in equipment manufacturing, component supply, technology R&D and other areas. Some Indian manufacturers need to realize that China's mature construction equipment industrial chain is not an obstacle to India's localization drive, but rather an important resource that can help India shorten its industrial upgrading cycle and improve manufacturing efficiency. How to cultivate independent innovation capacities through opening-up and cooperation is an important question for India's construction equipment industry as it moves toward global competition. For India, the yardstick for manufacturing success should not be merely how much its import dependence has fallen, but whether its companies can build sustainable technological advantages and competitiveness in the international market. Self-reliance does not mean self-isolation, and localization should not become synonymous with protectionism.
